# Marked entropy: local attainment and its exact directional value formula

This is a bounded consequence of the actual full-space contact certificate.
It concerns a finite marked entropy problem, not the optimized mixed depth
itself. It proves local positive attainment, a body-domain comparison, and the
exact directional formula with the MINIMUM over all old contact certificates.
No parameter derivative or minimax interchange is assumed.

The finite sampled-majorant argument is the same mechanism independently
identified by Defect and the contributor and proved in
`candidate 87de5b3c068291f1`.
The additional ingredients here are a uniform
bound from marked values alone, entropy maximizer compactness, and an exact
identification of the finite-dimensional superdifferential.

## 1. Setting and statement

Let P be a fixed finite complete base, and K_z positive full-dimensional convex
d-fibers, d>=1, forming the actual compatible canonical hull
C=conv union_z({z} x K_z). Put dm=sum_z dX|K_z and M=sum_z |K_z|.
Take a positive continuous concave L on C with

    (1/M) integral_S log L dm=0.

Fix finitely many marks Y_i=(p_i,y_i), with y_i in int K_(p_i), and write
l_i=L(Y_i)>0. Suppose L has an actual contact certificate at these marks:
there are sigma_i>=0 summing to one and, for each positive sigma_i, probability
rows rho_i such that

    E_(rho_i) w=Y_i,
    E_(rho_i) L=l_i,
    sum_i (sigma_i/l_i) rho_i=dm/(M L).                (1)

Zero weights can be omitted or retained. The finite-source transport theorem
and the contributor's global multiplicative inequality are the audited dependencies
`candidate 3b257d8ddacb6167`
and `candidate b2578378c7102b3c`.

For b=(b_i)>0 define the marked entropy

    H_C(b)=sup_U (1/M) integral_S log U dm,             (2)

where U is positive continuous concave on C and U(Y_i)<=b_i for every i.
There is no logarithmic normalization imposed on U in (2). The old certificate
gives H_C(l)=0 and the unique maximizing sampled restriction is L.

Let K_z(t) be actual compatible positive fibers on the same P, converging to
K_z, and retain the SAME marks Y_i; they lie in their current fibers for small
t. Write C_t and dm_t for their canonical hull and mixed measure. In the
moving problem use the FIXED old denominator M:

    H_t(b)=sup_U (1/M) integral_(S_t) log U dm_t,
                   U(Y_i)<=b_i.                     (3)

Assume a signed bounded radial first-speed path: the old/current radial
functions about fixed interior origins differ by O(t), their quotients have
surface-almost-everywhere first limits corresponding to inward normal speeds
v_z, and the usual bounded domination holds. These are the hypotheses of
`candidate d750a370b2e831ee`;
only its elementary continuous-integrand shell formula is needed here. Put

    s(v)=(1/M) sum_z integral_(boundary K_z) log L(z,X) v_z(X) dS.

Let C(L,Y) be the set of ALL certificates (1), with their weight vectors sigma,
on these fixed marks. Then, for b_i(t)=l_i+t h_i+o(t),

    H_t(b(t))
       =t[-s(v)+min_(sigma in C(L,Y)) sum_i sigma_i h_i/l_i]
                +o(t).                               (4)

The minimum is attained. The conclusion is unchanged to first order if the
current mean 1/M_t is used instead of 1/M, because H_0(l)=0.

For all sufficiently small body/bound perturbations, (3) has a positive
continuous maximizing parameter. It can be chosen as the minimum of at most
the number of marks affine functions, with uniformly bounded coefficients
and a common positive floor on the old and current canonical hulls. Its
sampled restriction converges uniformly to L. No assertion about a unique
extension between sampled fibers is made.

## 2. The sampled-majorant lemma

Suppose U is positive continuous concave on a current canonical hull, all
sampled values are at most B, and every mark has a fixed-radius ball in its
own fiber. Choose an own-fiber supergradient c_i of U at Y_i. Positivity on
that ball implies |c_i|<=B/r_i. Define

    phi_i(z)=max_(X in K_z(t))[U(z,X)-c_i.X].

Actual anchored compatibility and concavity of U show that phi_i is sampled
concave: whenever q=sum lambda_z z,
phi_i(q)>=sum lambda_z phi_i(z). The own-fiber supporting inequality gives
phi_i(p_i)=U(Y_i)-c_i.y_i.

There is a finite base slope alpha_i satisfying

    alpha_i.(z-p_i)>=phi_i(z)-phi_i(p_i) for every z.  (5)

Indeed the finite Farkas obstruction would be nonnegative coefficients with
sum lambda_z(z-p_i)=0 and sum lambda_z[phi_i(z)-phi_i(p_i)]>0; normalization
would contradict the just-proved sampled concavity at p_i. Choose the
minimum-norm solution in aff(P)-aff(P). The constraint matrix is fixed and
the right side is bounded by B and the common body radius. The fixed-matrix
Hoffman bound, or equivalently the finite active-set formulas for the
minimum-norm feasible point, bounds alpha_i uniformly. This remains valid at
a boundary base and in lower affine rank.

The plane

    A_i(z,X)=U(Y_i)+alpha_i.(z-p_i)+c_i.(X-y_i)

majorizes U on every S_t fiber and touches it at Y_i. Thus

    V=min_i A_i >=U on S_t,    V(Y_i)=U(Y_i),          (6)

and the coefficients of these finitely many planes are uniformly bounded.
Each A_i is positive on the sampled fibers and hence on their convex hull,
so V is a positive continuous concave feasible parameter there.

The planes are only required to majorize sampled fibers. No nonexistent
ambient supergradient of U at a boundary base is used. In particular the
supremum phi_i, rather than a guessed affine extension of c_i, supplies the
base slope.

Applying this lemma to the OLD L gives a finite-plane V>=L on S, touching
all marked bounds l_i. the contributor's certificate implies mean log(V/L)<=0, whereas
V>=L gives the reverse inequality. Hence V=L on every sampled fiber. We may
therefore replace the old unsampled extension by this finite-plane positive
representative. It has a common positive concave extension to a neighborhood
of C, which will be used as an actual comparison parameter on C_t. All
quantities in (1)--(4) are unchanged by this replacement.

## 3. Bounded marked values control all sampled maxima

This step prevents a hidden compactness assumption in the entropy problem.
Write q_i=d(sigma_i bar_rho_i)/d(dm/M), where
bar_rho_i=(L/l_i)rho_i. Thus q_i>=0, sum_i q_i=1 almost everywhere, and

    (q_i/L)dm=(M sigma_i/l_i)rho_i.                   (7)

No smoothness of q_i is needed.

For every positive conditional tilted row on fiber z, let

    g_iz=E_(rho_i)[X | Z=z].

It belongs strictly to int K_z: a nonzero absolutely continuous measure on a
full-dimensional convex body cannot have its barycenter on a supporting
hyperplane. There are only finitely many relevant pairs. Choose a common
small contraction a_t->0, large enough compared with the fiber Hausdorff
error that

    T_i,t(z,X)=(z,(1-a_t)X+a_t g_iz)

maps every row's old fiber support into K_z(t). The conditional centroids
preserve each full row barycenter EXACTLY:
E_(rho_i) T_i,t w=Y_i. This uses tilted conditional means, not original-volume
means or an affine centroid graph.

For any U feasible for (3), row Jensen gives

    (1/M) sum_zi integral_(K_z) q_i U(T_i,t w)/L(w) dm
         <=sum_i sigma_i b_i/l_i.                    (8)

Choose a fixed positive-volume compact core D_z inside each old K_z. All
T_i,t(D_z) lie in a common fixed interior core of K_z(t) for small t. Any
positive concave U satisfies

    U(x)>=(dist(x,boundary K)/diam K) max_K U.          (9)

To see this, express x as a convex combination of a maximum point and the
other endpoint of the line segment in K; the coefficient of the maximum is
at least dist(x,boundary K)/diam K. Thus U(T_i,t w)>=c_z max_(K_z(t)) U
for w in D_z, with c_z>0 independent of U and t. By (7), sum q_i=1 there;
L is bounded above. Therefore (8) yields a UNIFORM bound on every sampled
maximum whenever b lies in a fixed compact subset of the positive orthant.

This argument is valid even when the density rows have arbitrary measurable
boundaries. It only uses their actual barycenters and domination by the old
mixed volume. All zero conditional rows can simply be omitted.

## 4. Local positive attainment and uniform sampled majorants

The old finite-plane L, multiplied by min_i b_i/l_i if necessary, supplies a
legal current competitor whose entropy tends to zero as (t,b)->(0,l).
The maximum bound from Section 3 bounds the entropy above. Consider any
entropy near-maximizing sequence with t->0 and b->l.

Its logarithmic integral is bounded below. Together with a uniform upper
maximum and positive lower fiber volumes, this bounds each fiber maximum
away from zero: if one maximum tended to zero, its whole logarithmic integral
would tend to minus infinity while all other fibers have a bounded positive
contribution. For a positive concave function with maximum m, homothety about
a maximizer gives

    |{U<s m}| <=[1-(1-s)^d]|K|<=d s|K|.

Consequently log U is uniformly integrable. In particular its absolute
integral on sets of volume h tends to zero uniformly, with bound
C h(1+|log h|). This also applies to the feasible majorants (6).

Replace each near-maximizer by its sampled majorant V_t. It remains feasible,
does not decrease entropy, and has finitely many uniformly bounded affine
coefficients. Pass to a subsequence of those coefficients. The resulting
finite-plane V is nonnegative on C, positive in every fiber interior, and
V(Y_i)<=l_i. Uniform logarithmic integrability and Hausdorff convergence give

    mean_old log V = lim mean_current log V_t >=0.

The old certificate gives mean log V<=0. Its multiplicative proof still
applies to a possible boundary-zero V: its logarithm is integrable, rows give
no mass to fiber boundaries, and its marked values are positive. Equivalently
apply it first to V+delta L and let delta decrease to zero. Equality plus
V(Y_i)<=l_i forces V=L almost everywhere; continuity of finite-plane functions
then gives equality on every sampled fiber, including its boundary.

Thus EVERY subsequential finite-plane majorant limit agrees with L on S.
The bounded coefficients and Hausdorff convergence imply uniform convergence
on old and current sampled fibers, and hence a common positive floor there.
Each constituent affine plane is at least their minimum on S; positivity
extends to the canonical hull. Bounded coefficients also extend this floor
to a fixed small neighborhood of C.

These arguments prove H_t(b)->0 as (t,b)->(0,l). They also prove local positive
attainment. To be explicit, at fixed nearby (t,b) take a maximizing sequence,
replace it by the bounded majorants, and take a coefficient limit. Logarithmic
uniform integrability preserves its optimal value. If there were arbitrarily
nearby (t,b) for which every such limit had a zero, choose a sequence approaching
(0,l) and approximating maximizing planes with minima tending to zero. The
preceding subsequential rigidity would force their limits to equal the
strictly positive L on S, a contradiction. Hence all sufficiently nearby
problems have a strictly positive maximizing finite-plane representative.

This is local attainment around a strictly positive certificate. It is not a
global attainment claim for arbitrary marked entropy data; positivity of
boundary limits would be unjustified without the certificate and its equality
case.

At each attained nearby problem the maximizing SAMPLED restriction is unique.
If two feasible maximizers differed on positive mixed volume, their arithmetic
mean would be feasible and strict concavity of log would increase the objective.
Equality almost everywhere upgrades to equality on each closed sampled fiber
by continuity. Consequently every exact nearby entropy optimizer has the same
sampled restriction as its finite-plane representative, and converges uniformly
through sampled boundaries. This does not extend to arbitrary near-optimizers,
which can retain the previously exhibited downward boundary layers.

## 5. The actual body-domain comparison

Let b(t)->l. Choose current entropy maximizers in the bounded finite-plane
class of Section 4. Call them V_t. They converge uniformly to L on the old and
new sampled fibers, have a common positive floor, and define positive concave
functions also on the old hull. They obey the SAME marked constraints there,
because the marks have not moved. Hence

    (1/M) integral_old log V_t <= H_C(b(t)).

The signed radial shell formula and uniform convergence give

    (1/M)[integral_current log V_t-integral_old log V_t]
          =-t s(v)+o(t).                              (10)

The replacement of log V_t by the fixed continuous log L costs o(1) times the
O(t) symmetric-difference volume, hence o(t); this is the essential uniform
boundary control. There is no derivative of V_t in (10). We obtain

    H_t(b(t))<=H_C(b(t))-t s(v)+o(t).

Conversely take old entropy maximizers for bounds b(t), again in the bounded
finite-plane class. They converge uniformly to L, are positive on the current
hull for small t, and satisfy its unchanged marked constraints. The same shell
calculation gives the reverse inequality. Therefore

    H_t(b(t))=H_C(b(t))-t s(v)+o(t).                  (11)

More generally, with only Hausdorff O(t) and no first speed, the body term is
the actual fixed-reference log-integral difference, with an o(t) error. No
artificial contraction speed or centroid drift appears. The contractions in
Section 3 were only a compactness estimate, not the body derivative.

## 6. The entire fixed-body superdifferential

H_C is finite and concave on the positive orthant. Finiteness above follows
already from (1): for marked bounds b, the certificate gives

    H_C(b)<=sum_i sigma_i log(b_i/l_i).

A positive constant competitor supplies a finite lower bound. Concavity follows
by mixing two admissible concave functions and using concavity of log. Therefore
H_C is locally Lipschitz, with a nonempty compact superdifferential at l.

For every contact certificate sigma in C(L,Y), its global multiplicative
inequality gives

    H_C(b)<=sum_i sigma_i log(b_i/l_i)
            <=sum_i (sigma_i/l_i)(b_i-l_i).

Thus (sigma_i/l_i) belongs to the superdifferential.

Conversely let g be any supergradient of H_C at l. Monotonicity gives g_i>=0.
The exact scaling law H_C(c b)=H_C(b)+log c, tested in both directions at c=1,
gives sum_i g_i l_i=1. For any continuous radial concave-parameter direction h
(h+cL concave for some c>=0), L+t h is positive concave for small t. The
supergradient inequality at its marked values implies

    sum_i g_i h(Y_i)>=(1/M) integral h/L dm.           (12)

Both affine signs give equal mass and full first moments; negative convex
tests give precisely the finite-source allocation condition. The audited
finite-source martingale theorem therefore supplies a martingale from
sum_i g_i delta_Yi to dm/(M L). Its two L moments equal one. Concave Jensen
then makes every positive row L-tight. Setting sigma_i=g_i l_i yields (1),
with nonnegative weights summing to one. Hence EXACTLY

    superdiff H_C(l)
       ={(sigma_i/l_i)_i : sigma in C(L,Y)}.          (13)

The set of certificate WEIGHT vectors is consequently compact; no compactness
of a chosen disintegration or uniqueness of the coupling is needed.

## 7. Directional formula and normalization

A finite concave function on an open finite-dimensional domain has right
directional derivative equal to the minimum of its supergradients on that
direction. Here this can be seen directly: every old supergradient bounds the
upper difference quotient. Supergradients at l+t h are locally bounded; any
subsequential limit is an old supergradient, and their supporting inequalities
at l bound the lower quotient. Thus (13) gives

    H_C(l+t h+o(t))
       =t min_(sigma in C(L,Y)) sum_i sigma_i h_i/l_i+o(t).

Local Lipschitz continuity permits the o(t) perturbation of the marked bounds.
Combining with (11) proves (4). This is an exact finite-dimensional
superdifferential calculation, not a swapped body/parameter minimax.

If the current denominator M_t is used, its supremum is exactly M H_t(b)/M_t.
Since M_t=M+O(t) and the value in (4) is O(t), this changes the formula by o(t).

The result describes the exact first-order marked entropy feasibility budget.
It does not itself prove a derivative of the optimized buffered-depth value:
that still needs the actual scalar/quantile inverse response linking marked
bounds to all halfspaces. It supplies no Gamma payment and does not identify
the volume certificate with an independently chosen surface transport.

## 8. An exact nonsmooth marked calibration

Take one interval K=[-1,1], M=2, L=1, and marks -1/2, 0, 1/2. Every old
certificate weight vector is

    (sigma_-,sigma_0,sigma_+)=(r,1-2r,r),  0<=r<=1/2.

Necessity follows from total mass and the mean zero of the uniform target.
For sufficiency use the uniform whole-interval row at mark zero and the
uniform left/right half-interval rows at the other two marks. The displayed
mixture has exactly the uniform target and the required row means.

If the two endpoint-mark bounds are both b_e and the center bound is b_0,
then EXACTLY

    H_C(b_e,b_0,b_e)=log min(b_e,b_0).

The r=0 and r=1/2 certificates give the two upper bounds; the constant
min(b_e,b_0) attains their minimum. Thus a directional minimum over different
certificates is genuinely necessary, even in one continuous dimension.

For arbitrary marked direction (h_-,h_0,h_+), formula (4) with fixed body gives

    H'_C(1;h)=min(h_0,(h_-+h_+)/2).

This can also be checked without the abstract derivative theorem. Put
A=min(h_0,(h_-+h_+)/2), B=h_+-h_-. The positive affine competitor
U_t(x)=1+t(A+B x) satisfies all three bounds 1+t h_i for sufficiently small t
and has entropy t A+O(t^2). The two certificate bounds give the matching upper
coefficient. No assertion of a unique derivative of the maximizing parameter
is needed.
